etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English londlord, landlorde, from Old English landhlāford, equivalent to land +‎ lord. Cognate with Scots landlaird, Middle Low German lantlord (“homeowner, landlord”).

definitions.definition: A person that leases real property; a lessor.

quote.citation: 1593, anonymous author, The Life and Death of Iacke Straw […], Act I:
quote.text: Brethren, brethren, it were better to haue this communitie,Then to haue this difference in degrees:The landlord his rent, the lawyer his fees.So quickly the poore mans ſubſtance is ſpent  […]

definitions.definition: (chiefly British) The owner or manager of a public house.

quote.citation: 1980, AA Book of British Villages, Drive Publications Ltd, page 102:
quote.text: When asked to explain why he became a landlord, he told the Archbishop of York it was so he could close the pub on Sundays, and suppress the profane language and singing that came through the bar windows.

definitions.definition: (surfing, slang, with "the") A shark, imagined as the owner of the surf to be avoided.
